item.title: Mortgage Rates Dip Slightly to 6.96% APR
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: Mortgage Rates Today, Friday, November 6: A Little Lower
Mortgage rates edged lower to 6.96% APR on Friday, November 6, according to Zillow data. The decline follows a tech stock sell-off that pushed investors toward bonds, lowering rates. A stronger-than-expected October jobs report, showing 165,000 new jobs and 4.1% unemployment, may slow the rate drop by reinforcing expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Rates are unlikely to change significantly over the weekend. Tomorrow’s jobs report could influence mortgage rates, as the Fed’s December meeting looms. Inflation data, including the November 10 Consumer Price Index, will also shape future rates. Homeowners considering refinancing may benefit from current rates, though lenders adjust pricing daily. Rate locks are recommended to protect against market fluctuations. Personalized quotes vary based on credit scores, down payments, and other financial factors.

item.title: Unreleased Anthropic Model Solves Quantum Computing Conjecture
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: An unreleased Anthropic model just helped solve a major quantum-computing question
Physical Superintelligence Inc. used an unreleased Anthropic model to prove the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, a 14-year-old problem in quantum computing. The conjecture, which questions when quantum computers can outperform classical ones, was resolved in three days using a research system developed by David Turturean. PSI stated the proof shows quantum advantages require specific structures, confirming long-suspected limitations. The breakthrough follows AI-driven math advances like OpenAI's solution to Navier-Stokes equations. Terence Tao called math's 'romantic era' over, while MIT research found 76% of grad students less motivated by AI progress. Researchers called the proof a 'huge result' resolving a decades-old question, noting its 'magical' integration of concepts. Anthropic declined to comment on the model used.

item.title: Spate of bomb threats poses serious challenge to airline industry
item.description:
Source: BBC News
Bomb threats targeting 12 airlines over four days have forced emergency measures, though all were hoaxes. Threats arrived via phone calls and emails, prompting airlines to divert flights, deploy military escorts, and conduct mid-air inspections. Some planes landed at alternate airports, including an Aer Lingus flight forced to land 1,000 km from its destination. Experts warn of the industry’s challenge in identifying perpetrators, with no credible intelligence on the culprits. Paul Mason, an aviation security expert, notes the random targeting and potential link to hybrid warfare tactics, though Russia denies involvement. The Aviation Security Act 1982 imposes life imprisonment for false threats endangering aircraft. Airlines face financial costs but are accustomed to diversions for technical issues or weather. Passengers may not learn of disruptions until disembarking, with no refunds likely as airlines bear no fault. Authorities emphasize the deterrent effect of severe penalties, warning that even misguided attempts to mimic threats could lead to prosecution.

item.title: Russian Extremist Group Denies Involvement in Hoax Bomb Threats to Italian Airports
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
The 'Male State', a Russian extremist group linked to Vladislav Pozdnyakov, denied sending hoax bomb threats to Italian airports that caused flight disruptions. The threats, including emails and phone calls, were sent to Aeroporti di Roma and other targets, falsely claiming explosives on flights. The group, banned in Russia in 2021, renamed itself 'Male Legion' and is active on Telegram. A Telegram account associated with Pozdnyakov mocked accusations, questioning if the group still exists. Italian media, including La Stampa, suspect the group is acting as Russia's 'armed wing'. Italy's defense minister warned of a 'hybrid threat' to Europe, citing recent cyber attacks and false alarms. Bellingcat previously labeled the group a 'vocal and vile online booster' of Russia's invasion. Authorities continue investigating whether the threats are coordinated or copycat actions. No explosives were found on any aircraft, and the origin of the emails, linked to Bogota's health services, remains unclear.

item.title: European Airlines Face New Wave of Bomb Threats
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines
European airlines faced a third wave of bomb threats this week, prompting flight disruptions and security responses. Flights to and from Lisbon, Rome, Prague, and Sofia were targeted, with three planes escorted by Hungarian fighter jets. Media outlets including Ireland's RTÉ were evacuated after receiving similar threats, though no direct links between airline and media incidents were confirmed. Nearly 30 aircraft and multiple airports were affected earlier this week, with the UK labeling the threats a 'malicious hoax.' Ryanair reported a targeted flight, while Czech Republic and Bulgaria saw at least 11 flights each targeted. France reported four flights under threat, all landing safely. No explosives were found. Irish authorities warned of a 'likely coordinated campaign of disruption,' with Prime Minister Micheál Martin calling the situation 'worrying.' Sky confirmed receiving a security threat, and the Russian group 'Male State' denied involvement, mocking accusations of responsibility. Authorities continue investigating the origin of the threats.

item.title: Train Collides With Truck at Carlsbad Crossing; Driver Injured
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Video shows train vs truck collision at Carlsbad crossing; driver suffers minor injuries
A Pacific Surfliner train collided with a white pickup truck at a Carlsbad railroad crossing just before 11 a.m. Monday near Grand Avenue and State Street. Video shows the truck, traveling the wrong way, stopped on tracks as the train struck it, sending the vehicle spinning. The female driver suffered minor injuries and was hospitalized. Sheriff's investigators confirmed the pickup was moving against traffic before attempting to cross after crossing arms had already lowered. Lori Winfree, deputy CEO of the North County Transit District, stated the crossing equipment functioned correctly and warned that ignoring warning signals remains a recurring issue. She urged compliance with railroad crossing alerts, emphasizing that down arms, bells, and flashing lights indicate an imminent train. Winfree advised drivers stranded on tracks to exit and move at a 45-degree angle away from the train to avoid debris. The incident underscores ongoing risks of disregarding railroad safety protocols.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV Tours South America After Lung Cancer Surgery
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News, Deutsche Welle, BBC News Original headline: Pope Leo Begins South America Tour Following Lung Cancer Surgery
Pope Leo XIV has begun a 12-day South America tour, his first major overseas trip since lung cancer surgery. The 71-year-old pontiff, who removed a right lung tumor last month, arrived in Uruguay after a 14-hour flight. Vatican officials confirmed he is fully recovered and requires no further treatment. 'I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward,' he told journalists. The tour includes Argentina and Peru, with 12 flights, two helicopter rides, 36 speeches, and visits to 10 cities. Uruguay, Latin America's most secular nation, was chosen as the first stop, drawing crowds of up to 30,000. In his first speech, Leo addressed Uruguay's secular traditions and liberal laws on abortion and euthanasia, emphasizing the importance of protecting family life. The visit includes stops in Casavalle, a poor neighborhood, and a prayer vigil at Centenario Stadium. The trip, covering over 20,000 miles, highlights his engagement with Latin America's 40% of global Catholics, despite declining church attendance.
item.source: NPR Topics: News, Deutsche Welle, BBC News

item.title: LA Sheriff's Department Targets Prohibited Deputy Cliques and Gangs
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Sheriff institutes new policy aimed at eliminating prohibited deputy cliques and gangs
Los Angeles County Sheriff Robert Luna announced a new policy targeting prohibited deputy cliques and gangs following his landslide reelection. The policy expands beyond previous measures by defining 'prohibited cliques' as unauthorized subgroups engaging in activities that harm employment or rights, including exclusionary behavior. Luna emphasized the policy’s goal to eliminate groups undermining accountability and public trust. The policy requires deputies to avoid participating in cliques and participate in investigations, with violations risking discipline. This builds on a 2024 policy banning gangs and hate groups. Critics like Robert Bonner, former head of the Sheriff Civilian Oversight Commission, praised the measure as necessary to eradicate deputy gangs. The policy addresses decades of organized deputy cliques, such as the Executioners and Vikings, linked to violence and intimidation. Legal settlements exceeding tens of millions have resulted from past incidents. The LA County Board of Supervisors plans to mandate gang disclosures. Luna has repeatedly vowed to eliminate such groups, with Bonner optimistic about the policy’s potential success if enforced effectively.

item.title: San Diego to Eliminate Historic General Fund Deficit
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: City of San Diego on track to eliminate 'historic' general fund deficit, according to new report
San Diego's CFO said the city's ongoing revenues will cover expenses without one-time funding. The city faces no deficit in FY28 after years of cuts and revenue gains. Deficits dropped from $136.8 million in FY25 to $88.8 million in FY27. The Five-Year Financial Outlook credits $323 million in annual improvements, including $180 million in cuts and $80 million from Measure B trash fees. Mayor Gloria called the balance 'structurally sound' but warned of remaining infrastructure needs. The city avoided service cuts by consolidating departments and reducing positions. Ongoing challenges include elevator repairs and unmet resource demands. The outlook sets the framework for next year's budget, with no surplus to spend.

item.title: El Niño-Driven Storms and High Tides Threaten Southern California
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Un cambio importante en la atmósfera abre el camino para que El Niño azote el sur de California
A powerful subtropical jet stream between Hawaii and California is channeling El Niño-driven storms toward the West Coast, intensifying rainfall and high tides. Scientists note El Niño's warm waters are releasing excess moisture, leading to stronger storms that could merge with king tides, causing severe flooding. Phil Gonsalves of the National Weather Service reported San Diego received double its usual October rainfall. Recent storms, dubbed 'pineapple express' events, have historically caused property damage and flooding in San Diego. High tides in La Jolla reached 2.77 meters (9 feet 0.98 inches) on Tuesday, the highest recorded since 1920, with ocean temperatures 10 degrees above average. Minor flooding occurred in Point Loma, Pacific Beach, and Mission Beach, while Waymo vehicles faced waterlogged streets. The National Weather Service warns of more king tides from November 24-26 and December 23-25 as El Niño strengthens. Reinhard Flick of Scripps Oceanography called the event unprecedented, with water levels 1.5 feet above normal. Gonsalves emphasized the unpredictability of weather systems, noting El Niño's impacts remain difficult to forecast precisely.

item.title: States vary in housing permit rates, affecting affordability
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: These maps show which states are actually building housing
Housing permits in the US remained flat from January to August 2026, with a 0.05% rise since 2025 but a 4.1% decline since 2023. Nicholas Irwin, research director at the Lied Center for Real Estate, said states are struggling to build enough housing, with some lagging behind. New York saw permit increases, while Nevada declined. Nationally, 968,187 permits were issued, averaging 2.83 units per 1,000 residents. South Carolina, Idaho, and North Carolina had the highest permit rates, double the national average. Alaska, Connecticut, and Illinois had the lowest. California's median homeowner income is $84,900 below what's needed to afford its median-priced home. In 31 states, median income falls short of affordability. Irwin urged states to build diverse housing and use local policies to boost affordability, noting state-level approaches vary widely.

item.title: US Urges China to Fulfill Busan Trade Deal Obligations
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: US asks China to uphold Busan trade deal commitments
US officials urged China to fully implement commitments under the 2025 Busan trade deal, including rare earth and mineral exports. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng via videoconference, emphasizing the need for China to meet obligations like purchasing 25 million metric tons of US soybeans over three years and resuming rare earth exports. The 2025 agreement, reached during Trump and Xi Jinping's Busan summit, capped US tariffs at 20% and suspended new Chinese export curbs. He expressed 'serious concern' over recent US trade restrictions, though both sides agreed to 'continuously strengthen cooperation.' The pact was extended until January 10 next year, with a planned APEC meeting in Shenzhen. China also confirmed discussions for a trilateral summit with Trump and Putin at the APEC gathering.

item.title: Two skydivers die during record attempt in Lake Elsinore
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: 2 skydivers killed while training for record-breaking maneuver in Lake Elsinore
Two women died Friday in Lake Elsinore during a skydiving training session aimed at setting a state record for the largest upright formation by women. Authorities reported the incident occurred in the 20000 block of Cereal Street, where deputies found the skydivers receiving medical aid before they were pronounced dead at a hospital. Chazi Rutz, a professional skydiver from Arizona, confirmed the group was attempting a 19-way formation, surpassing the existing 12-way record. The accident happened after the skydivers deployed their parachutes, with Rutz stating they became entangled due to proximity. Rutz described the women as experienced and passionate about the sport, emphasizing the tragedy of the accident. The investigation into the incident is ongoing. Earlier incidents in Lake Elsinore include a 2023 case where a solo skydiver avoided injury after hitting power lines and a May 2024 accident in Perris that resulted in one death and one injury.

item.title: Russian Diesel Tankers Divert from US Destinations
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Tankers carrying Russian diesel to the US change course
Sanctioned Russian diesel tankers diverted from US destinations, according to marine data firm Kpler and vessel tracking site MarineTraffic.com. Two tankers originally bound for US east coast instead headed to Brazil and Mediterranean, while a third changed course to a vague 'for orders' destination. The shift follows US President Donald Trump's recent easing of sanctions on Russian oil to secure diesel amid domestic price spikes. Russia denied the reports, with envoy Kirill Dmitriev calling the claims 'fake' and Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov stating shipment details were 'commercial' and confidential. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill warned port operators to reject Russian fuel, citing legal sanctions and congressional import bans. Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal also urged shipping firms to avoid violating sanctions, emphasizing no president can override existing statutes.

item.title: Health ISAC warns of cyberattacks on refrigeration systems after French blood bank breach
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: Health intel-sharing group warns industry in wake of cyberattack on French blood bank
Health ISAC, a healthcare-focused cybersecurity group, issued a warning about cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers, including a French blood bank. The bulletin highlights how operational technology (OT) attacks on refrigeration systems pose risks to healthcare, where temperature-controlled storage is critical for blood and vaccines. A French blood bank, the French Blood Establishment, was hacked via a vendor, causing temperature thresholds to rise but preventing damage through timely detection. The FBI, CISA, and other agencies released a fact sheet on threats to industrial refrigeration systems. Cybersecurity experts note vulnerabilities in refrigeration controllers, with some attacks possibly linked to Russian-aligned groups or Iran. The attacks exploit exposed systems, weak security, and AI-driven methods. Health ISAC urged hospitals to isolate refrigeration systems from hospital networks, use physical safeguards, and maintain offline backups. Experts warn patching OT systems is challenging due to downtime risks and outdated equipment. The incident underscores the need for global intelligence sharing to mitigate threats to critical infrastructure.

item.title: Gas Prices in San Diego Drop 40 Cents, Analysts Predict Further Decline
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Los precios de la gasolina en San Diego han bajado 40 centavos por galón en el último mes. ¿Qué pasará ahora?
Gas prices in San Diego dropped 40 cents per gallon in the last month, reaching $6.01 on average. Analysts attribute the decline to seasonal demand shifts, refinery maintenance, and California’s early switch to a cheaper winter gasoline blend. Governor Gavin Newsom ordered the transition a month ahead of schedule, which DeHaan, an energy analyst, said explains most of the drop. However, geopolitical tensions could reverse the trend. Oil prices fell 7% after reports of U.S.-Iran diplomatic talks, with Brent crude at $104 and West Texas Intermediate at $96.46. DeHaan predicts prices could near $5 per gallon in California by Christmas if peace talks succeed, but warns of potential volatility. High diesel prices, now $8.34 in California, also impact transportation costs, contributing to inflation. The Strait of Hormuz and Russia-Ukraine conflicts have further strained global supply chains, with analysts calling the past eight months the most volatile in their 25-year career.

item.title: Southwest Flight Diverts to LAX After Engine Issue
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Southwest flight from Orange County declares emergency, lands at LAX
Southwest Airlines Flight 3396 declared a general emergency shortly after departing John Wayne Airport and diverted to Los Angeles International Airport. The flight, scheduled to land at San José Mineta International Airport, stopped climbing around 20,000 feet and transmitted an emergency code to air traffic control. It took off at 11:30 a.m. and landed safely at LAX around 12:25 p.m. local time. The FAA stated the crew reported an engine issue, prompting the diversion. Southwest Airlines confirmed the pilots received an engine-related maintenance indication, leading to the safe landing on Runway 25L. LAX noted the flight landed without incident. The incident is under further investigation.

item.title: Sen. Blakespear Awards $1 Million to Solana Center for Waste Diversion Programs
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Solana Center for Environmental Innovation receives $1 million check presented by Sen. Blakespear
Sen. Catherine S. Blakespear, D-Encinitas, presented Solana Center for Environmental Innovation a $1 million check on Oct. 27 to expand waste diversion programs. The funding comes from the 2026-27 state budget. Blakespear praised the center’s role in climate solutions and sustainability, stating the grant supports innovative programs to advance California’s circular economy. Jessica Toth, Solana Center’s executive director, noted the funding enables projects to reduce landfill waste and promote reuse. The grant will develop models for the San Diego region and beyond to minimize garbage disposal. The center aims to make landfills obsolete through practical, scalable solutions. The funding supports waste diversion initiatives aligned with state environmental goals.

item.title: Octopuses' Squeezing Ability Inspires Robot Design
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Science Original headline: How octopuses squeeze through teeny tiny holes
Researchers studying octopus movement aim to improve robot design for search-and-rescue operations. Wenci Xin and Tamar Gutnick observed how octopuses navigate tight spaces, testing common and Mayan octopuses in a Vienna aquarium. The animals used a methodical process: extending an arm through a hole, assessing the space, then pulling their body through by compressing their body cavity. Mayan octopuses avoided holes smaller than the distance between their eyes, while common octopuses used all eight arms to force their way through. The findings suggest robots could mimic this 'pulling' approach instead of traditional pushing mechanisms. Engineer Mishu Duduta highlights the potential for robots to handle delicate tasks, not just dangerous ones. The study, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, could lead to more agile robots for exploring disaster sites or sunken shipwrecks.

item.title: California Waters Host Unusual Marine Life Surge
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Original headline: The Waters Off California Are Unrecognizable
Tropical marine life is migrating north along California's coast due to record-breaking warm waters from this year's intense El Niño. Scientists report species like whale sharks, manta rays, and reef fish typically found in the Sea of Cortez are now appearing in Southern California. Mike Couffer, a biologist, describes the phenomenon as 'just nuts,' noting the balmy waters have imported an entire ecosystem. NOAA researcher Owyn Snodgrass documents unprecedented warmth, with November 3 temperatures reaching 75°F—11°F above average. Fishermen have caught record-sized tuna, including a 650-pound bluefin, while tropical fish like the longfin bigeye, usually found in Mexico, are now common. However, warming waters threaten kelp forests, which support species like rockfish and sea otters. Sea turtles, including olive ridleys, are nesting in California for the first time, likely due to warmer temperatures. Federal officials are monitoring the nests, with plans to relocate eggs if needed. Scientists warn that this El Niño is a preview of future climate impacts, with some species potentially establishing new habitats in California.

item.title: Driver killed, two kids injured after sedan collides with school bus in Potrero
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune
A sedan collided with a school bus on state Route 94 near Plaskon Lane in Potrero on Friday around 3:40 p.m., killing the sedan driver and injuring two children. The crash, described as head-on, involved the bus colliding with a pole. Cal Fire spokesperson Capt. Josh Cormode confirmed the sedan driver died, while two of the approximately 35 students from Potrero Elementary School sustained minor injuries and were hospitalized. Cormode noted arrangements for parent pickup were being made, with the school and San Diego County Office of Emergency Services notified. The highway remained closed in both directions, and CHP urged drivers to avoid the area as crews worked to reopen the road. Details about the crash were not immediately released.

item.title: Carlsbad Community Rebuilds After Día de los Muertos Ofrenda Vandalized
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Community comes together in solidarity after Día de los Muertos ofrenda is vandalized
A Carlsbad community is rebuilding after its annual Día de los Muertos ofrenda was vandalized, leaving shattered photographs and broken structures. Community members gathered for a vigil to honor loved ones and begin restoration, emphasizing unity against hate. The ofrenda, a four-year tradition of marigolds, candles, and family photos, was destroyed over a weekend, with Sandra Carmona describing the damage as 'complete chaos.' Families viewed the destruction as deeply personal, with one member noting a grandfather's portrait was part of the tradition's origins. Despite the setback, residents vowed to continue the tradition, with David Hernandez planning a larger display next year. Carlsbad police are investigating the vandalism, which remains unsolved. A GoFundMe campaign aims to cover $5,000 in damages. Community leaders stress the ofrenda's role in preserving cultural heritage, calling it 'the one little space in all of Carlsbad that still holds that culture.'

item.title: Storm Causes 1-in-1,000 Flood in Tennessee and Georgia, Moves Up Atlantic Coast
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Storms that caused 1-in-1,000 year flood event in Tennessee and Georgia move up Atlantic coast
A storm system that triggered a 1-in-1,000 year flood along the Tennessee-Georgia border moved up the Atlantic coast, prompting flood advisories from North Carolina to Massachusetts. In McCaysville, Georgia, and Copperhill, Tennessee, residents and crews cleaned up after rainfall of 10.28 inches in six hours and 11.19 inches in 12 hours. The Toccoa River overflowed, leading to rescues by swift-water teams and leaving downtown streets submerged. At least one death occurred when Julie Barrs, 56, drove through floodwaters in Georgia. This marks the second major flood in three months for the communities, with McCaysville having reopened its police building just weeks prior. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp declared a state of emergency for four counties. A curfew remains in effect, and access to downtown is restricted. Police Chief Michael Otis Earley emphasized community resilience, stating, 'This disaster does not define who we are... how we move forward will define us.' Local businesses, including the Copperhill General Store, reported widespread damage. The towns, with populations under 1,500, rely on scenic railroads for tourism, now disrupted by the floods.
